blocks.text:
Design the core dispatch engine behind a food delivery service (the kind that powers Swiggy or DoorDash style delivery matching). The distinguishing challenge is capacity-aware batched dispatch: a delivery partner is not limited to one order at a time, they can carry several orders concurrently up to a fixed capacity, and the system must always assign a new order to the nearest partner that still has room, not simply the nearest partner overall.

  • Actors: Customer (places orders), DeliveryDispatchService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: restaurants, delivery partners with a capacity limit, nearest-available-partner dispatch, and the full order lifecycle through delivery.

The distinguishing mechanic is capacity-aware dispatch: the nearest partner is chosen only among those with spare capacity, letting one partner carry multiple orders as a batch, and completing a delivery frees that partner's capacity for the next dispatch.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Place an order: a customer orders from a restaurant, to be delivered to their location.
Dispatch an order: assign the order to the nearest delivery partner that still has spare capacity.
Batch orders: a delivery partner may carry more than one order at a time, up to their capacity.
Track the order lifecycle: an order moves through placed, assigned, picked up, and delivered.
Free capacity on delivery: completing a delivery reduces that partner's current load, making them eligible for a new dispatch again.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting thousands of concurrent orders and partners must not require touching existing dispatch logic.
Extensibility: a new dispatch algorithm (route-optimized, surge-aware) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: dispatch rules, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: finding the nearest available partner is proportional to the number of partners currently tracked.
Thread safety: two orders dispatched to the same partner concurrently must never both slip past that partner's capacity check.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should distance be computed as straight-line (as the crow flies) or actual road-network travel distance?
Can a partner reject an assigned order, and if so, how should the system react?
Should batched orders be constrained to restaurants near each other, or is any combination under capacity acceptable?
Is there a maximum wait time before a stuck, undispatched order should be escalated or refunded?
Should partner capacity vary by vehicle type (bicycle versus car), or is it a fixed constant for this design?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Distance is computed as straight-line Euclidean distance on a flat coordinate plane, a simplification versus real road-network routing.
A partner cannot reject an assigned order in this design; order reassignment is noted as a follow-up.
Any combination of orders can batch onto the same partner as long as capacity allows, with no proximity constraint between the batched restaurants themselves.
Partner capacity is a fixed constant per partner, set at partner registration time.
A dispatch that finds no partner with spare capacity fails immediately rather than queuing for a retry.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Restaurant, DeliveryPartner, Order, and Customer

items: Restaurant: a location that prepares orders.
DeliveryPartner: a courier with a location, a capacity, and a current load.
Order: one delivery request, tracking its restaurant, assigned partner, and lifecycle status.
Customer: the destination of a delivery.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A restaurant prepares many orders; each order is assigned to at most one partner; a partner carries many orders up to capacity; an order is delivered to a customer

items: Restaurant to Order is one-to-many.
DeliveryPartner to Order is one-to-many, bounded by the partner's capacity at any given moment.
Order to Customer is many-to-one, a customer can place many orders over time.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep dispatch rules, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: how a partner is chosen for an order is exactly the kind of decision a real business would want to tune over time, starting simple and evolving toward smarter routing.

metadata.alt: DispatchStrategy interface with NearestPartnerDispatchStrategy as the concrete implementation

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a future route-optimized or surge-aware dispatch algorithm is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to the core assignment logic in DeliveryDispatchService. What it solves: it isolates partner-selection rules from the shared, stable assignment and lifecycle-tracking algorithm.
Why needed: a partner being assigned, a dispatch failing, or an order being delivered are all events a real delivery app would want to react to (customer notifications, partner apps, analytics).

metadata.alt: DeliveryObserver interface notified by DeliveryDispatchService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: DeliveryDispatchService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core dispatch workflow from side effects.
Why needed: order id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: OrderIdFactory generating sequential ORD prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every order is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Restaurant: attributes restaurantId, name, locationX, locationY; responsibility: represent one place orders are prepared.
DeliveryPartner: attributes partnerId, name, locationX, locationY, capacity, currentLoad; responsibility: track one courier's location and current carrying load.
Order: attributes orderId, restaurantId, customerName, destinationX, destinationY, assignedPartnerId, status; responsibility: represent one delivery request through its lifecycle.
DeliveryDispatchService: the orchestrator; responsibility: dispatch orders, enforce capacity, and track lifecycle transitions.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: DispatchStrategy and DeliveryObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: DispatchStrategy: findPartner(restaurant, partners): abstracts away exactly how a partner is selected for an order.
DeliveryObserver: onPartnerAssigned / onDispatchFailed / onOrderDelivered: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a first assignment to an empty partner, a second order batching onto an already-loaded partner, and capacity being freed on delivery.

metadata.alt: The first order dispatched finds the nearest partner, P3, who starts with zero load
Once P3 is full, the next nearest partner with spare capacity, P1, is chosen, carrying two orders at once
Delivering an order reduces that partner's load, making them eligible for a new dispatch again

blocks.text: The dispatch-then-lifecycle workflow, alongside its failure branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Dispatch finds the nearest partner under capacity, assigns and increments load, then pickup and delivery eventually free that capacity again

items: Happy path: dispatch an order → a partner with spare capacity exists → the nearest such partner is chosen → assigned, load incremented → partner picks up, then delivers → load decremented.
Batching path: dispatch a second order while the nearest partner still has spare capacity → it is assigned to the same partner, now carrying two orders at once.
Failure path: dispatch an order → every partner is already at full capacity → dispatch fails without assigning anyone.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: dispatchOrder(orderId): assigns the order to the nearest partner with spare capacity, or fails if none exists.
assignManually(orderId, partnerId): directly assigns an order to a specific partner, still capacity-checked.
markPickedUp(orderId): transitions an assigned order to picked up.
markDelivered(orderId): transitions a picked-up order to delivered, freeing the partner's capacity.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: NoPartnerAvailableException: every registered partner is already at full capacity.
InvalidOrderStateException: a lifecycle transition is attempted out of order, such as marking delivery before pickup.
PartnerCapacityExceededException: a manual assignment targets a partner who is already full.

blocks.text: The critical race is two orders dispatched to the same partner at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to assign an order to the same partner; synchronization ensures one assignment increments load before the other reads the current load

blocks.text: Synchronizing the check-then-increment step per partner ensures two concurrent dispatches can never both read a load just below capacity and both proceed, which would otherwise let a partner exceed their capacity.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new dispatch algorithm (route-optimized batching, surge-aware pricing tie-in) is a new DispatchStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (customer push notification, partner app alert) is a new DeliveryObserver implementation.
Partner rejection and reassignment can be added as a new lifecycle transition without touching the dispatch algorithm itself.
Vehicle-type-based capacity can be layered on by deriving capacity from a partner attribute instead of a flat constant.
Single Responsibility: DeliveryPartner tracks location and load, DispatchStrategy decides partner selection, DeliveryObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new dispatch algorithms or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to DeliveryDispatchService.
Liskov Substitution: any DispatchStrategy or DeliveryObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: DeliveryObserver exposes only the three lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: DeliveryDispatchService depends on the DispatchStrategy and DeliveryObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A partner exactly at their capacity limit is correctly excluded from being chosen for a new dispatch, not just partners already over it.
Delivering an order the moment a partner is at exactly zero remaining capacity immediately makes that partner eligible for the very next dispatch call.
Two orders from different restaurants can legitimately batch onto the same partner, since this design places no proximity constraint on batched orders.
A dispatch attempt when zero partners are registered at all fails the same way as when every partner is full, both reported as NoPartnerAvailableException.
dispatchOrder: O(p) where p is the number of registered partners, scanned to find the nearest one with spare capacity.
markPickedUp / markDelivered: O(1).
Space: O(restaurants + partners + orders) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Restaurant, DeliveryPartner, and Order

items: An index on DeliveryPartner(currentLoad, capacity) speeds up scanning for partners with spare capacity.
Order stores both restaurantId and partnerId as foreign keys, capturing the full assignment relationship for one delivery.
Move from straight-line distance to real road-network travel time for partner selection.
Support partner rejection with automatic reassignment to the next-nearest available partner.
Add a proximity constraint between batched orders, so a partner is never asked to travel in two very different directions at once.
In a distributed deployment, shard partner tracking by geographic region rather than scanning every partner for every dispatch.

// Lifecycle status of a single order.
enum OrderStatus { PLACED, ASSIGNED, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED }

// A place that prepares orders, at a fixed location.
class Restaurant {
    private final String restaurantId; // unique id
    private final String name;           // display name
    private final double locationX;        // x coordinate
    private final double locationY;          // y coordinate

    public Restaurant(String restaurantId, String name, double locationX, double locationY) {
        this.restaurantId = restaurantId; // store id
        this.name = name;                   // store name
        this.locationX = locationX;           // store x
        this.locationY = locationY;             // store y
    }

    public String getRestaurantId() { return restaurantId; } // id getter
    public double getLocationX() { return locationX; }          // x getter
    public double getLocationY() { return locationY; }             // y getter
}

// A courier with a location, a capacity, and a current load.
class DeliveryPartner {
    private final String partnerId;   // unique id
    private final String name;          // display name
    private final double locationX;       // x coordinate
    private final double locationY;         // y coordinate
    private final int capacity;               // max concurrent orders this partner can carry
    private int currentLoad;                    // orders currently being carried

    public DeliveryPartner(String partnerId, String name, double locationX, double locationY, int capacity) {
        this.partnerId = partnerId; // store id
        this.name = name;             // store name
        this.locationX = locationX;    // store x
        this.locationY = locationY;      // store y
        this.capacity = capacity;          // store capacity
        this.currentLoad = 0;                // starts empty
    }

    public String getPartnerId() { return partnerId; }     // id getter
    public double getLocationX() { return locationX; }        // x getter
    public double getLocationY() { return locationY; }           // y getter
    public int getCapacity() { return capacity; }                   // capacity getter
    public int getCurrentLoad() { return currentLoad; }                // load getter
    public boolean hasSpareCapacity() { return currentLoad < capacity; } // true if room for one more
    public void incrementLoad() { currentLoad++; }                          // take on one more order
    public void decrementLoad() { currentLoad--; }                             // free up capacity after delivery
}

// One delivery request, tracking its restaurant, assigned partner, and lifecycle status.
class Order {
    private final String orderId;         // unique id, e.g. ORD1
    private final String restaurantId;       // which restaurant prepared it
    private final String customerName;         // who receives it
    private final double destinationX;            // x coordinate of the delivery address
    private final double destinationY;               // y coordinate of the delivery address
    private String assignedPartnerId;                   // which partner is carrying it, if any
    private OrderStatus status;                            // current lifecycle state

    public Order(String orderId, String restaurantId, String customerName, double destinationX, double destinationY) {
        this.orderId = orderId;             // store id
        this.restaurantId = restaurantId;     // store restaurant
        this.customerName = customerName;       // store customer
        this.destinationX = destinationX;         // store destination x
        this.destinationY = destinationY;           // store destination y
        this.status = OrderStatus.PLACED;             // starts placed, unassigned
    }

    public String getOrderId() { return orderId; }                            // id getter
    public String getRestaurantId() { return restaurantId; }                     // restaurant getter
    public String getAssignedPartnerId() { return assignedPartnerId; }             // assigned partner getter
    public void setAssignedPartnerId(String partnerId) { this.assignedPartnerId = partnerId; } // assign a partner
    public OrderStatus getStatus() { return status; }                                 // status getter
    public void setStatus(OrderStatus status) { this.status = status; }                  // status setter
}

// Creates sequential, correctly-prefixed ids for orders.
class OrderIdFactory {
    private int orderCounter = 0; // running id counter

    public String nextOrderId() {
        orderCounter++;               // bump id counter
        return "ORD" + orderCounter;    // e.g. ORD1
    }
}

from enum import Enum

# Lifecycle status of a single order.
class OrderStatus(Enum):
    PLACED = "PLACED"
    ASSIGNED = "ASSIGNED"
    PICKED_UP = "PICKED_UP"
    DELIVERED = "DELIVERED"

# A place that prepares orders, at a fixed location.
class Restaurant:
    def __init__(self, restaurant_id, name, location_x, location_y):
        self.restaurant_id = restaurant_id  # unique id
        self.name = name                      # display name
        self.location_x = location_x            # x coordinate
        self.location_y = location_y              # y coordinate

# A courier with a location, a capacity, and a current load.
class DeliveryPartner:
    def __init__(self, partner_id, name, location_x, location_y, capacity):
        self.partner_id = partner_id  # unique id
        self.name = name                 # display name
        self.location_x = location_x       # x coordinate
        self.location_y = location_y         # y coordinate
        self.capacity = capacity               # max concurrent orders this partner can carry
        self.current_load = 0                    # starts empty

    def has_spare_capacity(self):
        return self.current_load < self.capacity  # true if room for one more

    def increment_load(self):
        self.current_load += 1  # take on one more order

    def decrement_load(self):
        self.current_load -= 1  # free up capacity after delivery

# One delivery request, tracking its restaurant, assigned partner, and lifecycle status.
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, restaurant_id, customer_name, destination_x, destination_y):
        self.order_id = order_id              # unique id, e.g. ORD1
        self.restaurant_id = restaurant_id      # which restaurant prepared it
        self.customer_name = customer_name        # who receives it
        self.destination_x = destination_x          # x coordinate of the delivery address
        self.destination_y = destination_y            # y coordinate of the delivery address
        self.assigned_partner_id = None                 # which partner is carrying it, if any
        self.status = OrderStatus.PLACED                  # starts placed, unassigned

# Creates sequential, correctly-prefixed ids for orders.
class OrderIdFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.order_counter = 0  # running id counter

    def next_order_id(self):
        self.order_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"ORD{self.order_counter}"  # e.g. ORD1

# Strategy interface: how a partner is chosen for an order.
class DispatchStrategy:
    def find_partner(self, restaurant, partners): raise NotImplementedError

# Picks the closest partner to the restaurant among those with spare capacity.
class NearestPartnerDispatchStrategy(DispatchStrategy):
    def find_partner(self, restaurant, partners):
        best = None                     # best candidate found so far
        best_distance = float("inf")      # distance of the best candidate
        for partner in partners:            # scan every registered partner
            if not partner.has_spare_capacity():
                continue  # skip partners already full
            dx = partner.location_x-restaurant.location_x  # x distance to the restaurant
            dy = partner.location_y-restaurant.location_y  # y distance to the restaurant
            distance = (dx * dx + dy * dy) ** 0.5  # straight line distance
            if distance < best_distance:  # closer than anything seen so far
                best_distance = distance  # remember the new best distance
                best = partner  # remember the new best partner
        return best  # the nearest partner with spare capacity, or None if none qualifies

# Observer interface: reacts to dispatch lifecycle events.
class DeliveryObserver:
    def on_partner_assigned(self, order, partner): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_dispatch_failed(self, order_id, reason): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_order_delivered(self, order): raise NotImplementedError

# Simple observer that prints events to the console.
class ConsoleDeliveryObserver(DeliveryObserver):
    def on_partner_assigned(self, order, partner):
        print(f"Order {order.order_id} assigned to {partner.partner_id}, load now {partner.current_load}")

    def on_dispatch_failed(self, order_id, reason):
        print(f"Dispatch failed for {order_id}: {reason}")

    def on_order_delivered(self, order):
        print(f"Order {order.order_id} delivered")

blocks.text: DeliveryDispatchService, including the auto-dispatch, manual assignment, and lifecycle transition logic:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class NoPartnerAvailableException(Exception): pass
class InvalidOrderStateException(Exception): pass
class PartnerCapacityExceededException(Exception): pass

# The core dispatch engine tying every piece together.
class DeliveryDispatchService:
    def __init__(self, strategy):
        self.restaurants = {}    # restaurantId -> Restaurant
        self.partners = {}         # partnerId -> DeliveryPartner
        self.orders = {}              # orderId -> Order
        self.strategy = strategy        # how a partner is chosen
        self.observers = []                # listeners

    def add_restaurant(self, restaurant):
        self.restaurants[restaurant.restaurant_id] = restaurant  # register a restaurant

    def add_partner(self, partner):
        self.partners[partner.partner_id] = partner  # register a partner

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def place_order(self, order):
        self.orders[order.order_id] = order  # register a new order
        return order

    def dispatch_order(self, order_id):
        order = self.orders[order_id]  # the order to dispatch
        restaurant = self.restaurants[order.restaurant_id]  # where it is being prepared
        partner = self.strategy.find_partner(restaurant, self.partners.values())  # ask the strategy for a partner
        if partner is None:  # nobody qualifies
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_dispatch_failed(order_id, "No partner with spare capacity")
            raise NoPartnerAvailableException(f"No partner available for order {order_id}")
        partner.increment_load()  # take on this order
        order.assigned_partner_id = partner.partner_id  # record the assignment
        order.status = OrderStatus.ASSIGNED  # advance the lifecycle
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_partner_assigned(order, partner)  # notify
        return order  # hand back the now-assigned order

    def assign_manually(self, order_id, partner_id):
        order = self.orders[order_id]  # the order to assign
        partner = self.partners[partner_id]  # the requested partner
        if not partner.has_spare_capacity():  # this partner cannot take more
            raise PartnerCapacityExceededException(f"Partner {partner_id} is already at capacity")
        partner.increment_load()  # take on this order
        order.assigned_partner_id = partner_id  # record the assignment
        order.status = OrderStatus.ASSIGNED  # advance the lifecycle
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_partner_assigned(order, partner)  # notify
        return order  # hand back the now-assigned order

    def mark_picked_up(self, order_id):
        order = self.orders[order_id]  # the order to advance
        if order.status != OrderStatus.ASSIGNED:  # must currently be assigned
            raise InvalidOrderStateException(f"Order {order_id} is not assigned, cannot be picked up")
        order.status = OrderStatus.PICKED_UP  # advance the lifecycle
        return order  # hand back the updated order

    def mark_delivered(self, order_id):
        order = self.orders[order_id]  # the order to advance
        if order.status != OrderStatus.PICKED_UP:  # must currently be picked up
            raise InvalidOrderStateException(f"Order {order_id} is not picked up, cannot be delivered")
        partner = self.partners[order.assigned_partner_id]  # the carrying partner
        partner.decrement_load()  # free up their capacity
        order.status = OrderStatus.DELIVERED  # advance the lifecycle
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_order_delivered(order)  # notify
        return order  # hand back the updated order

items: Why check capacity before distance rather than the other way around? Because a partner who is closest but full cannot actually take the order, so filtering by capacity first keeps the distance comparison meaningful, only comparing partners who could realistically be assigned.

Why allow batching with no proximity constraint between the batched orders? Because this design intentionally keeps the dispatch algorithm simple, real systems typically add a maximum detour constraint, explicitly called out as a follow-up rather than silently ignored.

How would you extend this to support partner rejection? Add a new lifecycle transition that reverts an ASSIGNED order back to PLACED and decrements the rejecting partner's load, then re-run dispatchOrder to find a new partner.

Nearest-available greedy dispatch vs global route optimization: greedy nearest-partner dispatch is simple, fast, and easy to reason about, at the cost of not finding the globally optimal assignment across all partners and orders at once; a full route-optimization solver could do better but is far more complex and slower to compute.

Fixed capacity per partner vs dynamic capacity based on order size: a fixed integer capacity is simple to check and reason about, at the cost of not accounting for the fact that some orders are bulkier than others; a weight or volume based capacity would be more realistic but adds meaningfully more bookkeeping.

Immediate dispatch failure vs a retry queue: failing immediately when no partner has capacity is simple and gives the caller a clear signal to act on, at the cost of not automatically retrying as partners free up; a retry queue would smooth over temporary capacity crunches at the cost of added complexity and latency.
Persist restaurants, partners, and orders in a database using the schema in the Database Design section, with partner location and load also cached in a fast key-value store for low-latency dispatch.
Emit dispatch and delivery events to a message queue so downstream systems (customer notifications, partner apps, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Shard partner tracking by geographic region in a large-scale deployment, so a dispatch call only scans nearby partners instead of every partner system-wide.
Track partner location via periodic GPS updates rather than a static coordinate, and re-run the nearest-partner search against the freshest available location.
